summary: Describes a mechanism for layer-2 separation of stations that reach an IPv4 gateway over a bridged Ethernet segment. It uses an ARP proxy function so that stations cannot talk directly to each other and all traffic goes through the gateway. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In an apartment building, every resident must send mail through the front desk rather than slip notes under each other's doors. This makes the network work the same way.

questions: how does mac-forced forwarding isolate customers
subtitle: Isolating customer networks on shared Ethernet access lines

tldr.problem: Broadband access networks need to keep customer traffic separate while sharing physical Ethernet infrastructure, and efficiently use IPv4 addresses by putting multiple customers in the same subnet.
tldr.mechanism: An Ethernet Access Node intercepts ARP requests from customers and replies with the gateway router's address instead, forcing all traffic between customers to go through the gateway. It also filters out direct layer-2 traffic between customers.
tldr.outcome: Customers cannot communicate directly at the Ethernet layer, preventing attacks and allowing the gateway to apply security policies. The mechanism trades some performance for strong isolation without requiring VLAN overhead.

facts.label: Access node role
facts.value: Ethernet bridge with ARP proxy and traffic filtering

facts.label: IPv6 support
facts.value: Unicast filtering only, multicast not filtered

today: RFC 4562 is Informational and describes a practical solution used in some broadband access networks. It has not been obsoleted. The mechanism remains relevant for Ethernet-based access as an alternative to PPPoE and VLAN-per-customer separation.

sections.title: The Access Network Challenge
sections.content:
Broadband access networks connect customers to service provider gateways. These networks have two parts: individual subscriber lines from each customer, and a shared aggregation network that collects traffic from many customers. The challenge is separating customer traffic at layer-2 (the Ethernet level) while efficiently assigning IP addresses from shared pools.

Historically, ATM-based networks solved this with separate virtual circuits per customer, but Ethernet as an access technology is cheaper and offers better multicast support for services like IPTV. Standard Ethernet switching, however, allows hosts in the same subnet to find each other directly at layer-2, which violates the isolation requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: A building uses a shared network to connect all apartments. The network needs to keep one apartment's traffic away from another's without using expensive isolation tricks.

sections.title: Why ARP Proxy Solves It
sections.content:
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is how devices find each other's layer-2 addresses (MAC addresses) when they know an IP address. Normally, an ARP request broadcast to find a peer's address gets an answer from that peer directly. MAC-Forced Forwarding intercepts these requests at the Ethernet Access Node (EAN) and replies with the gateway router's address instead.

This trick makes all hosts in the same subnet think the gateway is the layer-2 destination for every other host in that subnet. Traffic that should go host-to-host is redirected to the gateway, where it can be routed back to the correct customer. The gateway's own ARP replies identify it properly, so hosts can send to it directly too.
sections.plainLanguage: When an apartment asks 'who is at address 10.1.2.5?', the building's network control point answers 'send it to me (the front desk).' That way traffic from one apartment to another always passes through the front desk first.

sections.title: How the Access Node Enforces It
sections.content:
The EAN must do three things: learn which gateway routers are assigned to each customer, proxy ARP to force traffic through them, and filter out any frames that break the rules.

The EAN learns the gateway's IP and MAC address by snooping on DHCP replies to the customer, or by consulting static configuration. When a host ARPs for any IP address in its subnet, the EAN intercepts and replies with the gateway's MAC address. The EAN also discards any unicast frames coming from a customer that are not destined to an allowed gateway, blocking attempts to bypass the routing.

Multicast is an exception: the EAN forwards upstream multicast (with IGMP snooping to trim unnecessary branches) because multicast is native to Ethernet and efficient for broadcasts. IPv4 multicast sources must tunnel through the gateway, ensuring they are authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: The control point keeps a list of which router goes with which apartment. When an apartment asks for a neighbor's address, the control point says 'send it to your router.' It also throws away any mail addressed directly to a neighbor, to force it through the router.

sections.title: Deployment and Resiliency
sections.content:
MAC-Forced Forwarding works with both static and DHCP address assignment. Static assignment requires the EAN to be pre-provisioned with gateway mappings. DHCP is easier: the EAN snoops DHCP replies to learn what gateway a host received, and can use DHCP Relay Agent Information (option 82) to tag subscriber line identifiers in DHCP requests.

The EAN is stateful: if it fails, customer hosts lose connectivity until it recovers. The risk is mitigated if the EAN stores its state database in persistent storage, allowing quick restoration after transient failures. For true redundancy, customers must multi-home to multiple gateways, or use Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) to provide an alternate gateway IP address.

An important note for gateway routers: they must not send ICMP redirects to hosts on the aggregation network, because traffic between hosts in the same subnet arrives on the same interface from which it was received (after the gateway routing decision), which would normally trigger a redirect.
sections.plainLanguage: If the control point crashes, apartments lose internet until it comes back up. To keep the disruption short, the control point saves its configuration. For better reliability, an apartment can be set up to reach multiple routers, or the routers can share an IP address that switches if one fails.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
MAC-Forced Forwarding is a security mechanism that prevents malicious customers from sending traffic directly to neighbors' Ethernet addresses. It enforces the same isolation as an ATM network or per-VLAN separation, without the VLAN scalability limits (a maximum of 4096 VLANs per Ethernet) or the multicast inefficiency of VLAN-per-customer.

The EAN must reject spoofed IP addresses (filtering based on the source IP of assigned hosts), discard DHCP server replies from subscriber lines, and rate-limit upstream broadcast packets. IPv6 multicast requires special handling: unlike IPv4, IPv6 depends on multicast discovery, so the EAN must not filter IPv6 multicast indiscriminately, though it may rate-limit it.
sections.plainLanguage: The control point stops bad apartments from pretending to be other apartments or from sending fake network control messages. It also watches for neighbors trying to flood the network with broadcast junk.
